Filter Behaviors

Filter Behaviors allow engineers to refine or suppress candidate state values during pipeline processing while strictly preserving structural type. Filters operate on the value being considered for the next state snapshot and determine whether, and in what form, that value may proceed to reduction.

Filter Contract Summary

  • Filters must be pure and side-effect free
  • Filters must not mutate the incoming value
  • Filters must preserve the structural shape and type of state
  • Filters execute in initialization order
  • Errors during filter execution propagate as Vault errors

The Filter contract guarantees that filter execution is deterministic and isolated. If a filter function throws an error, that error is promoted to a Vault error and immediately terminates the current pipeline execution. The in-flight candidate value is discarded, no reducers are executed, and no snapshot is emitted. This ensures that filter failures never result in partially refined state or inconsistent pipeline outcomes. For details on how referential isolation is enforced at every stage boundary, see Pipeline Isolation.

Filters never mutate existing state, never influence pipeline scheduling or control flow, and never emit snapshots directly. Their sole responsibility is to refine or suppress the candidate next value before reduction.

Filter Stage

The Filter Stage runs after the resolve and merge stages and before reducers and taps. Filters receive the candidate next value produced by earlier stages and may refine or suppress that value while strictly preserving its structural type.

A filter may:

  • Return the value unchanged
  • Return a modified value with the same structural shape
  • Return undefined, which suppresses the update and prevents snapshot emission

Filters must be pure. They may not mutate the incoming value, and they may not change its structural type. Arrays must remain arrays, objects must remain objects, and primitives must retain their original primitive type. Structural violations result in controlled Vault errors to protect pipeline integrity.

Core Pipeline Stage

The Filter stage is a core pipeline stage and is always present as part of the FeatureCell lifecycle. However, individual filter functions are not registered as part of the FeatureCell’s declarative configuration. Instead, filter functions are attached exclusively through the fluent .filters() API during FeatureCell initialization, ensuring that value refinement and suppression rules are defined explicitly at startup rather than embedded into static cell configuration.

Fluent Filters() API

A FeatureCell may declare multiple filters. The fluent .filters() API accepts an array of filter functions, which is treated as a declarative, ordered configuration. When provided, filters are executed in the Processing Layer in the exact order they are listed during initialization.

An empty filter array is ignored and has no effect on pipeline execution.

Engineer-Supplied Filter Functions

Filter functions are supplied by engineers during FeatureCell initialization and execute exclusively within the Filter stage. Each function is evaluated as a pure, deterministic operation that must preserve the structural contract of the state. Filter functions do not own pipeline flow, scheduling, or lifecycle concerns; their sole responsibility is to accept, refine, or suppress the candidate value presented to them.

Although multiple filter functions may be composed, filter logic should remain narrowly focused and structurally conservative. Overly complex or interdependent filters can obscure intent and make rejection or transformation behavior difficult to reason about. Filters are most effective when each function enforces a single, clearly defined invariant.

Filter Stage Diagram
Available Filter Behaviors

The Filter behavior is part of the core pipeline and always present as a stage. Engineers supply filter functions that are executed by the core filter behavior during pipeline processing.

Core Filter Behavior
Behavior Description

withCoreFilterBehavior

input: candidateValue, filterFn

Executes an engineer-supplied pure filter function against the candidate next value. The filter function may refine the value or suppress it by returning undefined.

  • Arrays must return arrays
  • Objects must return objects
  • Primitives must retain their primitive type

Structural mismatches produce controlled Vault errors. This stage is ideal for conditional acceptance, sanitization, clamping, or value refinement without altering state shape.

FeatureCell Initialization

The Filter stage exposes a fluent configuration API that allows engineers to register filter functions during FeatureCell initialization.

This API does not execute filters directly. It records an ordered set of filter functions that are later applied by the Filter stage during pipeline execution.

Fluent Filter Configuration
Fluent API Description

.filters(filters)

input:

  • filters: FilterFunction<T>[]

returns: FeatureCellBaseShape (chainable)

Registers filter functions for a FeatureCell. The supplied functions define how candidate pipeline values may be refined or suppressed before reaching reducers and taps.

Filters are executed in the Processing Layer in the exact order they are registered. This method must be called before initialize(). Multiple calls overwrite prior filter configuration.

Filter Function Patterns

The Filter behavior is a core pipeline construct, but the filter functions they execute are supplied by engineers. While JavaScript allows many ways to express a function, only a small subset of patterns are safe and appropriate for use in the Filter stage.

From the pipeline’s perspective, there are only two dimensions that matter:

  • Whether the function depends on instance state
  • Whether the function is deterministic for a given input

The following categories describe the supported and discouraged ways to supply filter functions, ordered from most to least preferred.

Category A: Pure / Context-Free Functions (Recommended)

Pure filter functions depend only on their input value and produce a deterministic output. They do not reference this, do not close over mutable external state, and are fully predictable across executions.

This is the safest and most reusable form of filter function and is recommended whenever possible.

Example 1: Pure Filter Function

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    (employees) => employees.filter(e => e.status === 'Active')
  ]
).initialize()
// Inactive employees are removed`}}

Example 2: Factory-Generated Pure Filter Function

{{`// Factory function produces a pure, parameterized filter
export function partialFilterStartDateAfter(cutoff: string) {
  const cutoffDate = new Date(cutoff);

  return (employees) =>
    employees.filter(e => new Date(e.hireDate) >= cutoffDate);
}

// Register the generated filter during initialization
<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    partialFilterStartDateAfter('2020-01-01')
  ]
).initialize()

// Employees hired before 2020-01-01 are removed`}}

Category B: Instance-Aware but Correctly Bound Functions (Acceptable)

Filter functions may reference instance state as long as they are correctly bound to the instance. These functions are deterministic per instance but must not be shared across FeatureCells.

This pattern is acceptable when filter logic depends on configuration or state owned by the containing class.

Example 3: Arrow Function Using Instance State

{{`readonly salaryThreshold = 80000;

readonly filterBySalary = (employees) => {
  return employees.filter(e => e.salary > this.salaryThreshold);
};

<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [this.filterBySalary]
).initialize()`}}

Example 4: Bound Instance Method

{{`public filterByCity(employees) {
  return employees.filter(e => e.address.city === 'New York');
}

<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [this.filterByCity.bind(this)]
).initialize()`}}

Category C: Inline Lambdas (Allowed, Use Sparingly)

Inline lambda functions are allowed, but they are easier to misuse. Because they are often written inline, it is easy to accidentally close over mutable variables or embed complex logic that is difficult to test or reuse.

Inline filters are best reserved for trivial, self-contained rules.

Example 5: Inline Lambda Filter

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    (value: number) => Math.min(value, 10)
  ]
).initialize()
// 15 → 10`}}
Filter Function Anti-Patterns

Category D: External Mutable State (“Standalone” Functions — Discouraged)

Functions that appear standalone but rely on external mutable state are unsafe. Their behavior can change based on call order, shared state, or concurrent execution, making them unsuitable for deterministic pipeline processing.

If a filter requires state, that state must be instance-scoped and explicitly bound. External mutable variables should never influence filter behavior.

Example 6: Discouraged External State Dependency

{{`let cutoffDate = new Date('2024-01-01');

<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    (employees) =>
      employees.filter(e => new Date(e.hireDate) >= cutoffDate)
  ]
).initialize()

// ❌ Behavior depends on external mutable state`}}
Filter Function Summary

Filter Function Comparison

The following table summarizes the practical differences between the filter function styles demonstrated above. While all valid examples may execute correctly, they differ in reusability, testability, and long-term safety.

Filter Function Characteristics
Dimension Examples 1 / 2
Pure Filter Functions 		Examples 3 / 4
Instance-Bound Functions 		Example 5
Inline Lambda 		Example 6
External Mutable State
Purity ✅ ⚠️ Instance-scoped ✅ ❌
Determinism ✅ ⚠️ Per instance ✅ ❌
Safety for Pipelines ✅ ✅ ⚠️ ❌
Reusability High Medium Low Low
Testability High Medium Lower Low
Risk of Accidental Closure Low Low Higher High
Intended Lifespan Long-lived Instance-limited Ephemeral Unpredictable
Recommended Usage Preferred Acceptable Use sparingly Discouraged

Summary Rule

Any filter function must either be referentially transparent or explicitly instance-scoped and bound. Functions that depend on external mutable state or unbound instance context introduce hidden coupling and should be avoided.

Examples

Filters are applied by supplying pure filter functions that operate on the candidate next value during pipeline execution. The following examples illustrate valid and invalid filter function behavior.

Example 1: Array Filter — Keep Only Even Numbers

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    (value: number[]) => value.filter(n => n % 2 === 0)
  ]
).initialize()
// [1 , 2, 3, 4] → [2, 4]`}}

Example 2: Reject Update

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    () => undefined
  ]
).initialize()
// any incoming value → update suppressed`}}

Example 3: Invalid Structural Change

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    (value: number[]) => 42
  ]
).initialize()
// ❌ throws Vault error — array structure must be preserved`}}

Example 4: Object Filter — Remove Sensitive Fields

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    (value: { id: number; name: string; password: string }) => {
      const { password, ...rest } = value;
      return rest;
    }
  ]
).initialize()
// { id, name, password } → { id, name }`}}

Example 5: Primitive Filter — Clamp Value

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    (value: number) => Math.min(value, 10)
  ]
).initialize()
// 15 → 10`}}
Filter Anti-Pattern Examples

The following examples demonstrate invalid filter function behavior. These patterns violate the Filter contract by mutating the incoming value or by returning a value that does not preserve the original structural type. Such violations are detected and rejected by the Vault to protect pipeline integrity and ensure deterministic behavior.

Example 6: Invalid — Mutating the Input

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    (current) => {
      current.count++; // ❌ mutation
      return current;
    }
  ]
).initialize()

// ❌ Vault error: filters must not mutate the incoming value`}}

Example 7: Invalid — Returning Wrong Shape

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.filters(
  [
    (current) => 123 // ❌ incorrect type
  ]
).initialize()

// ❌ Vault error: filter returned incompatible value type`}}
